item.title: Honda says it may not build new plant in North America without trade deal extension
item.description: A senior Honda executive said the Japanese automaker might not build an eighth assembly plant in North America unless a key trade deal is extended.
item.dc:creator: Reuters Staff
item.content:encoded: A senior Honda executive said the Japanese automaker might not build an eighth assembly plant in North America unless a key trade deal is extended. The Trump administration is currently negotiating with Canada and Mexico over the fate of the free trade deal known as USMCA. Honda Executive Vice President Noriya Kaihara told reporters at a roundtable in Washington the automaker is close to full production capacity in North America and needs a new factory. However, “if there is no USMCA agreement in the future, we may have to change our direction,” Kaihara said, adding the company will need to make a decision within a year or two and would like the plant to be running by around 2030. He said currently Honda is not passing on the costs of tariffs to buyers in North America. The U.S. imposed 50 per cent tariffs on US$20 billion of Canadian products on Saturday, and Canada said it was retaliating effective September 8. Last year, Hyundai Motor told the administration that uncertainty about USMCA was delaying its investment decisions. “Early confirmation of USMCA’s extension would immediately unlock over US$20 billion in new American investments,” the automaker said in November. “Every month of ambiguity slows job creation, site selection and technology development.” With interest in Honda’s hybrid and other fuel-efficient models soaring as oil prices have remained high since the start of the U.S. war with Iran, the automaker had its best July in seven years, with car sales up 36 per cent. Honda in May scrapped its long-term EV sales target, including its goal of having EVs make up a fifth of its new car sales in 2030. It now plans 15 new hybrids by 2030. The Japanese automaker indefinitely suspended its Canada EV project, an US$11 billion investment plan to produce EVs and batteries. It also canceled three planned EVs for the U.S. market. Last year, Honda said it was shifting production of its U.S.-bound five-door Civic hybrid model from Japan to Indiana. (Reporting by David Shepardson; Editing by Chizu Nomiyama and Jan Harvey)

item.title: SpaceX to build US$100 billion Starship rocket complex in Louisiana
item.description: SpaceX unveiled plans on Tuesday to build a Starship rocket launch complex in southern Louisiana, a US$100 billion effort poised to transform coastal wetlands into a critical base for the company’s AI ...
item.dc:creator: Reuters Staff
item.content:encoded: WASHINGTON - SpaceX unveiled plans on Tuesday to build a Starship rocket launch complex in southern Louisiana, a US$100 billion effort poised to transform coastal wetlands into a critical base for the company’s AI satellite launch ambitions. The 125,000-acre (50,585-hectare) site on Pecan Island, which SpaceX named Starbase, La., will expand the company’s Starship launch operations beyond South Texas and Florida. It will eventually launch thousands of Starship flights a year, SpaceX president Gwynne Shotwell said. Construction will begin next year with the first Starship launch in 2029, SpaceX said in a statement. Shotwell detailed the plans near the proposed site in Louisiana’s Vermilion Parish at an event with Gov. Jeff Landry and other senior state officials. SpaceX plans to build a “self-sustaining” spaceport with its own propellant production, power generation, deep-water shipping capabilities, vehicle processing facilities, and probably an airport, Shotwell said. The marshland site is more than eight times the size of Manhattan. SpaceX has significantly expanded its U.S. South footprint in recent years, having built a Colossus AI data centre in Tennessee and Mississippi and Starlink facilities in Austin, Texas. It is planning a chip plant in central Texas. Landry called the deal an “inflection point” for Louisiana. “This project means more than just steel, technology, and capital. It represents jobs for our families. It represents momentum for our communities, and it represents protection for our coast,” he said. SpaceX said the Louisiana site will add more than 3,000 jobs to the region. SpaceX has faced backlash, however, from many residents near its sites concerned about water, environmental pollution and pressure to sell land. SpaceX has for years launched rockets from Cape Canaveral, Fla., Vandenberg Space Force Base in California and Starbase, the company town in South Texas that has been home to its Starship development and test-launch operations. (Reporting by Joey Roulette; Editing by Mark Porter and Rod Nickel) Joey Roulette, Reuters

item.title: ‘Really destructive for the Canadian steel industry,’ union warns as trade war escalates
item.description: Thousands more jobs could be at risk as U.S. President Donald Trump continues to escalate trade pressure on Canada, warns the United Steelworkers union.
item.dc:creator: Anam Khan
item.content:encoded: Thousands more jobs could be at risk as U.S. President Donald Trump continues to escalate trade pressure on Canada, warns the United Steelworkers union. The Canadian steel industry has already seen roughly 2,000 layoffs since the U.S. imposed a 50 per cent tariff on Canadian steel imports last year, says Meg Gingrich, assistant to the national director at the union, which represents 850,000 members across North America, including 225,000 in Canada. “Our members are often working for industries where the employer is the largest employer in the community. Those are community-sustaining jobs,” Gingrich told BNN Bloomberg. “It’s not just our members’ livelihoods at risk. It’s the full communities.” On Monday, Trump threatened to impose a 50 per cent tariff on all Canadian steel, vehicles, and auto parts starting Jan. 1, 2027. The tariffs would build on the existing tariffs already in effect that apply differently depending on the product class, as Canadian steel already faces a 50 per cent levy while non-U.S. automobiles and parts are currently subject to a 25 per cent tariff. Gingrich says while there is still uncertainty whether Trump will follow through, the incoming tariffs would be “really destructive for the Canadian steel industry,” as the uncertainty itself is taking a toll on workers. “It’s a psychological impact as well. As much as we have these supports and we can do domestically, it’s been really tough on our members and continues to be,” says Gingrich. ‘Canada has never been the problem’: U.S. workers The United Steelworkers union leadership has been very vocal in opposing U.S. tariffs on Canadian steel and goods. A month ago, the international presidents of the United Steelworkers union and the International Association of Machinists wrote a joint letter to U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer calling on the Trump administration to drop its tariffs on Canadian goods. “Canada has never been the problem,” said Roxanne Brown, international president of United Steelworkers. “Our two nations share a deep collaboration built on decades of economic integration as well as intelligence and defense cooperation. Rather than imposing further tariffs through Section 338 or any other mechanism, we should instead work together with our Canadian allies to limit illegal trade practices and advance our shared prosperity.” Union calls for more ‘Buy Canadian’ policies Gingrich says the union is calling on Ottawa to take a three-pronged approach to supporting the industry, including enhanced worker support, stronger industrial policies and a broader trade strategy aimed at preventing Canadian producers from being undercut by cheaper foreign steel. The union is also pushing for more Buy Canadian procurement policies and Gingrich says the priority should be to “keep people tied to their jobs.” The federal government has already taken a step in that direction. On Monday, the Canadian federal government announced it is investing $11.3 billion to build six new program icebreakers for the Canadian Coast Guard. This contract uses Canadian steel to support local workers, aiming to protect or create about 5,000 jobs. Gingrich called the move a positive sign. “I think there’s always more that we can do,” she says. “We have commitments to large infrastructure projects, and we want to make sure that Canadian products, Canadian-made steel, aluminum, other products, are going into that.” Stay strong on counter measures The union is also calling for Canada to remain prepared to use trade counter measures against the U.S. while protecting the domestic market from unfairly traded steel. “Historically, where we’ve seen a lot of the steel coming in, there’s just too much that’s produced in the world. A lot of it’s by China. A lot of it goes through other countries, Vietnam, Turkey,” says Gingrich. “I could keep naming more, but the main thing is to protect the domestic industry.” At the same time, she says Canada needs to balance those protections with its push to diversify trade beyond the U.S. “We want to make sure that we’re not doing it in a way where we end up allowing for tariff-free access to our markets for our products that we do produce here that would then end up hurting workers in Canada.”
